title: Kingston Police officer cleared by SIU after responding to stabbing
article: The province's Special Investigations Unit has cleared the Kingston Police officer who first responded to a fatal stabbing last September.

"I am unable to find that the deadly force used against the complainant (Evan Freeman) was excessive or unjustified," Joseph Martino, director of the SIU, said in his analysis. "Therefore, (I) have no reasonable grounds to believe that the subject officer committed a criminal offence in relation to the discharge of his firearm and the subsequent death of the complainant."
Martino noted that the officer's actions saved his and two other lives that day.

"Hopefully there is some closure now for involved members," Cam Gough, Kingston Police Association president, said on Monday. "Their actions that day, and Const. Fil Wisniak in particular, no doubt saved the lives of other innocent pedestrians.
"The city of Kingston should be proud of the Kingston Police as an organization in the way we responded."

On Sept. 12, 2019, at 1:43 p.m., the dispatch centre at the Kingston Police received a 911 call stating that a man, later identified as 22-year-old Freeman, was stabbing another man at the intersection of Queen and Bagot streets.

It has since been revealed that Freeman first attacked and killed 40-year-old Christopher Groeneveld-Barry just outside 121 Queen St. He then turned his attention to Terry Stafford, 85, who had just left his home for a walk. Stafford was stabbed twice in the face.
The next day, Stafford described the incident as a blur. He underwent oral surgery and received several stitches in his mouth and face.
The SIU report states that at 1:44 p.m., a pedestrian flagged down Wisniak, who was on patrol in the area.

Wisniak was the first officer to arrive at the scene and found Freeman still on top of Stafford. The report states that Wisniak ran toward Freeman while drawing his 9-mm Glock 22 pistol and notifying police dispatch that he was on scene.

The report said Wisniak repeatedly shouted at Freeman to get down on the ground while Freeman responded, "F- you" as he walked away from Stafford. Freeman first ran a short distance up Queen Street, then back to the intersection again toward a woman who witnesses reported appeared to be trying to help Groeneveld-Barry.

As Freeman approached the woman, she ran up Bagot Street as Wisniak continued to yell to Freeman. Freeman then suddenly turned and ran toward Wisniak, coming within a couple of metres. Wisniak backpedalled, and then fired a single round into Freeman's abdomen.
The report states Freeman was seen grabbing his stomach, but he still ran toward Wisniak. Wisniak backed away from Freeman twice before two more officers arrived in a Kingston Police SUV.

As those two officers exited the SUV with their weapons drawn, Freeman backed away, toward a flowerbed at 121 Queen St. Still holding the knife, Freeman stabbed and slashed himself in the neck multiple times.
Wisniak and another officer used their conducted energy weapon to stop Freeman, disarmed him and then started life-saving measures.
The entire altercation took less than a minute.
In investigating the incident, the SIU interviewed Wisniak and reviewed his notes. They also interviewed four other police officers and 22 civilian witnesses.

Investigators also received numerous pieces of materials from Kingston Police and the civilian witnesses. Two of the witnesses had created drawings of the scene and they used cellphone footage, showing nearly the entire incident, that had been submitted through the SIU's website.
The coroner found that Freeman died of a combination of stab wounds to his neck and the gunshot wound.
Wisniak has since been nominated for a Police Association of Ontario Hero of the Year award for his actions.
The life of Groeneveld-Barry was celebrated a week later.

Janet Barry, Groeneveld-Barry's mother, said after the ceremony that her family has the upmost respect for the police and what they were forced to do that day. She said her son would have been the first to forgive his attacker.

"There was nothing that could have prevented his death," Janet said. "He was in the wrong place at the wrong time. There are no guarantees as to how much time any one of us has on this earth. Chris knew that, and he believed strongly in the life-death continuum."

Janet and her husband, Cor Groeneveld, spoke to the Whig-Standard a month after their son's death. In that month, they had learned that Freeman had been involved with four provincial ministries: Education; Children, Community and Social Services; the Solicitor General; and the Ministry of Health. All of which, Janet said, had failed to support him.

"The (social supports) system is broken, and if anything optimizes that, it's this murder," Barry said. "This is the time to do a forensic review on (Freeman), on his life and on the systems that were involved with him, so we can figure out how we can do better.
"If people don't want to do that, then what does that say about us? What does it say about our systems and our society?"
